lines.text: Every structure this course has built so far answers the same kind of question by comparing whole keys, or whole values, against each other.
Here's a different question entirely: given a string, where does it live, found out one character at a time instead of comparing it whole against anything else?
A trie stores the characters themselves in its nodes, not the keys — each node has one child for every possible next character.
Walking from the root one character at a time either lands on the string or proves it was never there, and two words that start the same way walk through the exact same shared node.

lines.text: Before the reveal, think about what actually changes if this dictionary gets much bigger.
Does a lookup that walks one character at a time even notice how many other keys are stored alongside it?
No. Each step only ever consumes one character and moves to exactly one child — that cost never once references how many other keys share the trie.
Add far more words to the same dictionary and this exact lookup costs exactly the same.

lines.text: Here's the part worth sitting with: every earlier chapter's own cost grew with how many keys were stored.
This is the first structure in the whole course where that stops being true — the cost depends only on the key's own length.
Before this reveal, picture one single node's own array of possible next characters, sized for the whole alphabet.
On a sparse dictionary, how many of those slots do you think actually get used?
Almost none of them. One node rarely has anywhere near enough distinct children to fill every slot the alphabet allows.
That's the trade an array makes: every slot gets allocated up front, whether or not anything ever lands in it.
An array child slot costs nothing to search — one direct step, no comparison at all.
And on the exact dictionary measured here, the overwhelming majority of those slots sit completely empty.
Same shared tree underneath, every time — only the way a single node stores its own children changes.
A hash table keyed by character, a sorted list searched by comparison, or a tiny three-child structure built around one character at a time — three more ways to hold exactly the same information.
Before this reveal: the array's whole advantage was one direct step, no comparison needed.
Can something that compares against just one stored character still keep that same one-step-per-character discipline, while using far less memory?
Yes. Comparing against a single stored character, instead of indexing into a slot for every letter in the alphabet, needs far less memory per node.
It still consumes exactly one character per step forward — it just gets there by comparison instead of a direct index.
This structure's own node holds exactly one character, one value, and three children: two of them compare against that same character, and the third moves forward to the next one.
Measured on the exact same dictionary as every other representation here, this one used less memory than all three of the others.
Here's what actually got measured, not assumed: real memory, in bytes, for every representation, on the exact same small dictionary.
The array representation came out the most expensive by a wide margin — and that wasted memory is the exact problem every later design this syllabus names, and skips, exists to solve.
